parts.title: Part 1 · Volunteering to visit older people
parts.context: You will hear a man phoning a charity to offer to become a volunteer.

script.t: Good morning, Silver Link Befriending Scheme, Karen speaking. How can I help?
Hi. I saw your poster at the health centre, and I'm interested in volunteering, visiting older people who live on their own.
Wonderful, we're always looking for new volunteers. I can take a few details now and then send you an application pack. Is that OK?
Sure.
Can I have your name, please?
Alex Brennan. That's B-R-E-N-N-A-N.
Thanks, Alex. And what do you do at the moment? Are you working or studying?
I finished my degree last year, and now I'm a trainee architect at a firm in the city centre.
Oh, interesting. So when would you be available? Most of our volunteers visit once a week for about an hour.
Weekdays are difficult because of work. On Sunday mornings I usually visit my own grandparents, so I'd say Saturday afternoons would suit me best.
Saturday afternoons, lovely. Now, we try to match volunteers with older people who share their interests. What sort of things do you enjoy?
Well, I like walking, but I suppose not everyone would be able to do that. And I'm not much of a gardener, I'm afraid. But I play a lot of chess, so I'd be very happy to play with someone.
Chess, that's great. We actually have a gentleman who's been asking for a chess partner for months. And do you speak any languages apart from English?
Yes, my mother's Polish, so I speak Polish fluently. I did some Spanish at school, but I've forgotten most of it.
Polish could be really useful. We have several Polish speakers on our list. Now, before you start, there are a few checks. We'll need two references.
Can one of them be from a family member?
No, I'm afraid they can't be from relatives. Ideally, one should be from your employer and one from someone who's known you for at least two years, like a former teacher.
That's fine.
All new volunteers also attend a training session. The next one's on the twelfth of May. That's a Thursday evening.
Hang on, let me check my diary. Yes, the twelfth is fine.
Great. It's usually held here at our office, but because we're having some building work done, this one will be at the town museum, in the education room on the ground floor.
The museum, OK. Do I need to bring anything?
Yes, you'll need to bring some photo identification, such as a passport or a driving licence. Oh, and proof of address too, like a recent bill.
OK, no problem.
And one last thing. We pay volunteers' travel expenses.
Oh, that's kind. How much is that?
It used to be up to six pounds per visit, but we've just increased it to eight, because bus fares have gone up.
That's very generous. Thank you.
Not at all. I'll post the application pack to you today, and please call me if you have any questions.

parts.title: Part 2 · A centre for young and old
parts.context: You will hear the manager of a community centre speaking to parents at an open evening.

script.t: Good evening, and thank you all for coming to this open evening at Oakfield House. My name's Ruth Ellis, and I'm the manager here. As most of you know, Oakfield is rather unusual, because it combines a nursery for children aged two to five with a day centre for older people, all under one roof.

The idea actually came about almost by accident. Originally, the council planned to build the nursery on a separate site across the road. But when that land turned out to be unsuitable, the only space available was next to the existing day centre, and so we decided to try sharing the building. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened.

People often ask who benefits most. We expected it to be the children, and they certainly do benefit, but in fact the biggest change we've seen is in the older people. Staff report that many of them are more active and more talkative than before, and some who rarely spoke to anyone now look forward to coming in every day.

Of course, safety is a concern for many parents. All our staff and volunteers have been through full background checks, and the children are always supervised by nursery staff. They're never left alone with the older visitors.

The two groups don't spend the whole day together. Each has its own space, and joint activities take place each morning. When we first opened, these sessions lasted the whole morning, but we found that was too tiring for both groups, so now they last about two hours.

The nursery staff have noticed two things in particular about the children. Firstly, they've become much more confident when talking to adults they don't know. And secondly, they've learned to be more patient, because some of the older people move and speak quite slowly. A few parents have told us that their children's reading has improved, but to be honest, it's too early to say whether that's because of the centre.

Now let me tell you about this term's joint activities. On Mondays, there's a singing session led by one of our day centre members, who used to work as a pianist in a hotel. He's wonderful with the children.
On Tuesdays, it's cooking. Last term the children and older people made biscuits together, but we decided they contained too much sugar, so this term they'll be making soup instead.
Wednesday is gardening. Normally that happens in the vegetable beds outside, but they're being rebuilt at the moment, so this term the sessions will take place in the greenhouse.

And on Fridays we have storytelling. The older people bring in old photographs and use them to tell the children about their own childhoods. It's always a favourite. Right, I'll now take you on a short tour of the building.

parts.title: Part 3 · A presentation on ageing populations
parts.context: You will hear two students, Priya and Ben, planning a presentation on how governments respond to ageing populations.

script.t: Priya, shall we sort out the plan for our presentation on ageing populations?
Yes, let's. First, sources. I found a government report on pensions that has some really useful data.
Great, let's definitely use that. I also watched an online lecture by a demographer, which explained the background very clearly. I think we should include it too.
Agreed. What about that newspaper article you mentioned?
I reread it, and it's more opinion than evidence, so let's leave it out. I also thought about interviewing our grandparents, but the tutor said personal stories wouldn't count as academic sources.
Fair enough. And the textbook chapter is a bit out of date. It was written before the latest population figures came out.
So, just the two sources, then. Now, the policies. Let's start with raising the retirement age.

Most economists support it, because people are living longer. The problem is that it's extremely unpopular. Whenever a government proposes it, there are protests, and politicians worry about losing elections.
Yes. And what about paying families to have more children?
From what I've read, births go up for a year or two, but then they fall back to where they were. People just have children earlier than they would have done anyway.
Right. Then there's using robots in care homes.

That's an interesting one. There have been a few trials, but nobody really knows yet whether older people accept them, or whether they actually save money. We'd need to see a lot more studies before we could say anything.
OK. And building housing designed for older people?
I like that idea, because if older people move into smaller homes, larger family houses become available, so younger families benefit as well.
Good point. And free public transport for older people?
Well, it sounds good, but the cost would be enormous, and I can't see any government affording it at the moment.
So how shall we organise the presentation? We could go country by country.
That might be repetitive, since many countries use the same policies. Why don't we organise it by policy, and give examples from different countries for each one?
Yes, that's much clearer. And we should remember the feedback from our last presentation.
Definitely. The tutor said we spoke clearly and kept to time, but our slides had far too much writing on them.
So this time, mainly pictures and key words. What should we do next? The slides are almost finished.

I think the most useful thing would be to rehearse. We could ask the tutor to watch us, but she's away this week. Shall I book one of the study rooms in the library for Thursday, and we can practise there?
Good idea. Let's do that. I'll email you the latest version of the slides tonight, so you can check them before Thursday.
Perfect. And if we have time afterwards, we could ask a couple of friends to watch and give us some honest feedback.

parts.title: Part 4 · Forecasting population
parts.context: You will hear part of a lecture on how population forecasts are made.

script.t: Good morning. Today's lecture is about population forecasting, in other words, how demographers try to predict the size and structure of future populations, and why their predictions sometimes turn out to be wrong.

All population forecasts are built on three components. The first is births, the second is deaths, and the third is migration, the movement of people into and out of a country or region. If we know how many people there are today and can estimate these three components, we can calculate how the population will change.

The most widely used technique is called the cohort-component method. Here, the population is divided into groups according to age and sex. Each group is then moved forward in time, year by year. For example, the women aged thirty this year become the women aged thirty-one next year, minus those who die or leave, plus those who arrive. Births are calculated by applying fertility rates to the women in each age group.

Of the three components, fertility is generally the hardest to predict. Death rates tend to change slowly and fairly steadily, but birth rates depend on personal choices, which can shift quite quickly in response to economic conditions or changing attitudes. That said, forecasters have also made mistakes about deaths. During the second half of the twentieth century, many forecasts underestimated the rise in life expectancy, because they assumed that improvements in health would slow down. In fact, they continued for much longer than anyone expected.

To understand long-term trends, demographers often refer to a model called the demographic transition. In the first stage, both birth rates and death rates are high, so the population grows slowly, if at all. In the second stage, death rates fall, mainly because of better sanitation and a more reliable food supply, while birth rates remain high. This is when populations grow most rapidly. In the third stage, birth rates also begin to fall, as women gain access to education and paid employment. And in the fourth stage, both rates are low. Some researchers have added a fifth stage, in which birth rates fall so low that the population begins to shrink.

This process has important consequences for the age structure of a population. As birth rates fall and people live longer, the proportion of older people rises. Economists pay particular attention to the ratio of retired people to workers, because it affects how pensions and healthcare can be paid for.

Given all this uncertainty, how should forecasts be presented? In the past, many organisations published a single figure for the expected population in, say, fifty years' time. Today, most forecasters prefer to give a range, showing the most likely outcome along with higher and lower possibilities. This is a more honest way of communicating what we do and don't know.

Finally, it's worth remembering that forecasts are not just academic exercises. Governments use them to plan services. If a forecast predicts more young children in a particular area, the local authority may decide to build new schools there. If it predicts more older residents, it may need to invest in care services instead. So the accuracy of these forecasts really does matter to people's everyday lives.

passages.title: Why are families getting smaller?
passages.subtitle: Demographers have identified several forces behind one of the most important social changes of modern times

paragraphs.text: Over the past half century, the average number of children per woman has fallen dramatically across most of the world. In many wealthy countries, the figure is now well below the level needed to keep a population stable in the long term without migration. More surprisingly, rapid declines have also taken place in many middle-income countries, often over a much shorter period than they took in Europe or North America. Demographers have spent decades trying to explain this shift, and while no single factor accounts for it, several broad explanations have gained wide acceptance. The change has been so widespread that it can now be found in almost every region, in rich and poor countries alike, and among people of very different cultures and religions.

The first concerns child survival. In societies where many children die young, parents tend to have large families, partly to ensure that some of their children survive to adulthood. In some cases, parents also had additional children to replace those they had lost. As healthcare and nutrition improve and child mortality falls, families no longer need to have as many children to achieve the family size they want. Historical records suggest that falls in child mortality have generally been followed, after a delay of one or two generations, by falls in birth rates.

A second explanation focuses on economics. In agricultural societies, children often begin contributing to the household from an early age, working in the fields or caring for animals. In urban, industrial economies, by contrast, children are expensive. They must be housed, fed and educated for many years before they become financially independent, and the cost of raising them tends to rise as parents invest more in each child's education. Economists describe this as a shift from quantity to quality, as parents choose to have fewer children but spend more on each one. In addition, pensions and other forms of social security have reduced the need for parents to rely on their children for support in old age.

Education, particularly the education of women, is widely regarded as one of the most powerful influences of all. Women who stay in school longer tend to marry and have their first child later, and they are more likely to work outside the home. Education also increases knowledge of family planning. Studies comparing regions within the same country have found that differences in women's schooling explain a large part of the variation in birth rates, even when differences in income are taken into account.

Cultural change also plays a part, though its effects are harder to measure. Television and, more recently, the internet have exposed people to different ideas about family life. In several countries, researchers have found that areas which gained access to popular television dramas featuring small families experienced faster declines in fertility than similar areas without such programmes. Changing attitudes to marriage and the growing importance of personal fulfilment have also been suggested as contributing factors.

Government policy can also influence birth rates, although not always in the way intended. In the past, some countries actively tried to reduce birth rates through public campaigns or even legal limits on family size. Today, others that are concerned about ageing populations and shrinking workforces are trying to raise birth rates by offering cash payments, longer parental leave or cheaper childcare. The results of such policies have generally been modest. Cash payments, in particular, appear to affect the timing of births more than the total number of children that families eventually have.

Many demographers now believe that the obstacles facing young adults deserve more attention. Surveys in a number of countries show that people would, on average, like to have more children than they actually do. The gap is often explained by practical barriers, such as the high cost of housing, insecure employment and the difficulty of combining a career with family responsibilities. If this is correct, policies that make it easier for young people to establish stable lives may prove more effective than direct financial incentives. In some countries, the average age at which women have their first child has risen by several years within a single generation.

Whatever its causes, the decline in birth rates is likely to have far-reaching consequences. Smaller generations of workers will need to support larger numbers of retired people, and some regions may face labour shortages and the closure of schools. Yet some researchers point out that smaller populations may also bring benefits, such as less pressure on natural resources and greater investment in each individual. How societies adapt will depend largely on the choices they make in the coming decades. Some governments are already preparing for these changes by encouraging people to stay in work for longer.

passages.title: Planning for longer lives
passages.subtitle: Experts from different fields consider how societies should adapt to rising life expectancy

paragraphs.text: In the middle of the twentieth century, a person born in a wealthy country could expect to live to around sixty-five. Today, a child born in the same country has a reasonable chance of celebrating a hundredth birthday. Improvements in nutrition, sanitation and medical care have all contributed to this change. This remarkable increase in life expectancy is one of humanity's greatest achievements, yet it has also created challenges that governments, employers and individuals are only beginning to address.

Traditional thinking divides life into three stages, namely education, work and retirement. This model was designed for a world in which retirement lasted only a few years. According to the economist Lena Marsh, it no longer makes sense when people may spend thirty years or more in retirement. She argues that a longer life should be seen as an opportunity to rethink the entire life course, with people moving between periods of work, study and rest at different ages rather than following a fixed sequence. In her view, the main obstacle is not human biology but the rigid structure of institutions such as pension systems and universities.

Not all experts share her optimism. The health researcher David Okafor points out that longer lives are not necessarily healthier lives. While average life expectancy has risen steadily, the number of years that people spend in good health has not always increased at the same rate. As a result, many people now spend a longer period at the end of their lives living with long-term conditions that require ongoing care. Okafor believes that unless far more is invested in preventing illness, rising longevity will place unsustainable pressure on health services. He also notes that the cost of such care is likely to rise further as treatments become more advanced.

The question of who will provide this care is becoming increasingly urgent. In many countries, care for older people has traditionally been provided by family members, most often women. However, smaller families, greater geographical mobility and the rising number of women in paid work mean that this informal system is under strain. The sociologist Hana Varga has studied communities in which older people support each other through organised networks of volunteers. She found that these schemes not only reduced loneliness but also delayed the point at which members needed professional care. In her opinion, such networks could become an essential part of the care system, although they cannot replace trained professionals entirely.

Housing is another area where change is needed. Most homes are designed for younger, able-bodied people, with stairs, narrow doorways and bathrooms that are difficult to use for someone with limited mobility. The architect Tomás Rivera argues that new homes should be built to be adaptable from the start, so that they can be modified easily as their occupants grow older. This, he claims, would add relatively little to construction costs and would allow many older people to remain in their own homes rather than moving into residential care. He also suggests that new housing developments should mix homes for different age groups, rather than concentrating older people in separate retirement villages.

The world of work will also need to adapt. As populations age, many employers are already facing shortages of experienced staff, and some have begun to recruit older workers actively. Research suggests that, contrary to popular belief, older employees are no less productive than younger colleagues in most types of work. Although they may be slower at some tasks, they tend to make fewer serious errors. Nevertheless, age discrimination remains widespread, and older job seekers often find it difficult even to obtain an interview. The management specialist Grace Lin argues that flexible arrangements, such as part-time contracts and gradual retirement, are the key to keeping older people in the workforce. Many older workers, she notes, do not want to stop working completely but would welcome a lighter workload.

Individuals themselves also face new decisions. A longer life requires more savings, and surveys suggest that most people are financially unprepared for a retirement that may last several decades. Financial advisers increasingly recommend that people start saving for retirement in their twenties. A longer life also raises questions about how people should invest in their own skills and health. If the three-stage life is giving way to something more flexible, then learning, saving and staying healthy can no longer be left to particular stages of life but must become lifelong activities.

A longer life, then, is neither simply a burden nor simply a gift. Whether it proves to be more one than the other will depend largely on how well societies prepare for it, and on whether they are willing to rethink institutions that were designed for a very different age.
